proposals.before: Their suppression of treachery and elimination of villains scarcely differed from the methods of Zhi Du and Ning Cheng.
proposals.after: Their suppression of treachery and elimination of villains was rather different from the likes of Zhi Du and Ning Cheng, was it not?
proposals.reason: Chinese 殆與郅、寧之倫異乎 is a rhetorical question implying contrast with Zhi Du and Ning Cheng, not near identity with them.

proposals.before: When Shusun Hou, an Attendant Secretary in the Palace, was briefly derelict in his inner duty, Ni punished him according to law.
proposals.after: When Shusun Houtou, Palace Minister, was briefly derelict in his inner duty, Ni punished him according to law.
proposals.reason: 殿中尚書 is Palace Minister, not Attendant Secretary; 叔孫侯頭 is the personal name Shusun Houtou, not Shusun Hou.

proposals.before: Shusun Hou, an Attendant Secretary in the Palace, had been derelict for a moment in his inner duty; Ni applied the law to restrain him.
proposals.after: Shusun Houtou, Palace Minister, had been derelict for a moment in his inner duty; Ni applied the law to restrain him.
proposals.reason: Same office and name errors as the idiomatic line: 殿中尚書 and 侯頭.

proposals.before: Because Yang Ni of northern Pingcheng was a distinguished scholar, Ni recommended him in a memorial.
proposals.after: Because Yang Ni of Beiping was a distinguished scholar, Ni recommended him in a memorial.
proposals.reason: 北平陽尼 is Yang Ni of Beiping, not northern Pingcheng.

proposals.before: Because Yang Ni of Pingcheng in the north was learned in scholarship, he submitted a memorial recommending him.
proposals.after: Because Yang Ni of Beiping was learned in scholarship, he submitted a memorial recommending him.
proposals.reason: 北平 is the commandery Beiping; the literal English splits it as Pingcheng in the north.

proposals.before: When he was about to suffer the law, Emperor Xiaowen came to the Taihua Palace to receive him in audience, sent an attendant to proclaim an edict reprimanding him, and then at his home granted him death by strangulation.
proposals.after: When he was about to suffer the law, Emperor Xiaowen came to the Taihua Palace to receive him in audience, sent an attendant to proclaim an edict reprimanding him, and then at his home granted him death.
proposals.reason: 賜盡 is an ordered suicide or bestowed death, not specifically strangulation.

proposals.before: During the Zhenjun reign he served as Protector-General of Didao and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Anyang.
proposals.after: During the Zhenjun reign he served as Protector-General of Didao and was enfeoffed as Baron of Anyang.
proposals.reason: Chinese 安陽男 is the noble rank nan (baron), not hou (marquis); the same biography later correctly uses 侯 for Marquis of Rencheng.

proposals.before: In the Zhenjun era he was Protector-General of Didao and was granted the noble rank of Marquis of Anyang.
proposals.after: In the Zhenjun era he was Protector-General of Didao and was granted the noble rank of Baron of Anyang.
proposals.reason: Chinese 男 is baron, not marquis.

proposals.before: He was thereupon styled the Empress Dowager's maternal uncle to Emperor Xianwen.
proposals.after: He was thereupon styled Emperor Xianwen's maternal uncle.
proposals.reason: 獻文親舅 means maternal uncle of Emperor Xianwen, not of the empress dowager; the idiomatic line already has this right.

proposals.before: When the imperial carriage reached Bingzhou he appointed Hongzhi General-in-Chief of Hexi to campaign against the mountain Hu.
proposals.after: When the imperial carriage reached Bingzhou he appointed Hongzhi commander of Hexi (dujiang) to campaign against the mountain Hu.
proposals.reason: 河西都將 is a campaign commander of Hexi, not 大將軍 (general-in-chief).

proposals.before: Zi Shen
proposals.after: His son Shen
proposals.reason: 子神 is 'son Shen' (the son's personal name 神), not a binome given name Zi Shen; the following unit identifies him as 長子神.

proposals.before: Zi Shen
proposals.after: His son Shen
proposals.reason: Same error as the idiomatic line: 子 marks kinship 'son', 神 is the name.

proposals.before: Shen of Changzi was bold and resourceful from youth and was renowned for spirited valor.
proposals.after: The eldest son, Shen, was bold and resourceful from youth and was renowned for spirited valor.
proposals.reason: 長子神 follows 子神 and 劉氏四子: 長子 is eldest son, not the county Changzi.

proposals.before: He first served as a Central Gentleman of Wuhui.
proposals.after: He first served as a Rapid-as-Tigers Palace Gentleman.
proposals.reason: 武卉中郎 is the office 武賁中郎 (hu ben), not a place or title Wuhui.

proposals.before: At that time the leading bandits of the capital region were known as Baozi and Biaozi. Both were skilled horsemen and archers who gathered between Lingqiu and Yingmen to rob and plunder.
proposals.after: At that time the leading bandits of the capital region were known as Baozi and Biaozi. Both were skilled horsemen and archers who gathered between Lingqiu and Yanmen to rob and plunder.
proposals.reason: 應門 in this Lingqiu pairing is 雁門 (Yanmen), not Yingmen.

proposals.before: Zan's wife was a sister of Emperor Zhuang and was later enfeoffed as Princess Chang of Xiangcheng; Zan was therefore posthumously granted the governorship of Ji Province.
proposals.after: Zan's wife was a sister of Emperor Zhuang and was later enfeoffed as Grand Princess of Xiangcheng; Zan was therefore posthumously granted the governorship of Ji Province.
proposals.reason: 長公主 is the rank Grand/Senior Princess, not a personal name Chang.

proposals.before: Zan's wife was a sister of Emperor Zhuang; later she was enfeoffed as Princess Chang of Xiangcheng, and therefore Zan was specially granted posthumous appointment as governor of Jizhou.
proposals.after: Zan's wife was a sister of Emperor Zhuang; later she was enfeoffed as Grand Princess of Xiangcheng, and therefore Zan was specially granted posthumous appointment as governor of Jizhou.
proposals.reason: 長公主 is a rank (Grand Princess), not the given name Chang.

proposals.before: His son Mao, courtesy name Zu'ang, inherited his father's noble rank.
proposals.after: His son Mao, courtesy name Zu'ang, inherited his grandfather's noble rank.
proposals.reason: 襲祖爵 is inheritance of the grandfather's (Cui Xuan's) noble rank, not the father's.

proposals.before: His son Mao, style name Zu'ang, inherited his father's noble rank.
proposals.after: His son Mao, style name Zu'ang, inherited his grandfather's noble rank.
proposals.reason: Chinese 祖爵 denotes the grandfather's noble title, not the father's.

proposals.before: Tian Shi, courtesy name Xianbiao, was a native of Xiayi in Fengyi.
proposals.after: Tian Shi, courtesy name Xianbiao, was a native of Xiagui in Fengyi.
proposals.reason: Chinese 下邽 is Xiagui, not Xiayi (下邑).

proposals.before: Tian Shi, style name Xianbiao, was a man of Xiayi in Fengyi.
proposals.after: Tian Shi, style name Xianbiao, was a man of Xiagui in Fengyi.
proposals.reason: Chinese 下邽 is Xiagui, not Xiayi.

proposals.before: Emperor Wu of Zhou heard of this and commended him, promoting him to Palace Attendant of the Third Rank, enfeoffing him as Duke of Xindu County, and appointing him governor of Yan Province.
proposals.after: Emperor Wu of Zhou heard of this and commended him, promoting him to Equal to the Three Excellencies, enfeoffing him as Duke of Xindu County, and appointing him governor of Yan Province.
proposals.reason: 儀同三司 is the prestige rank Equal to the Three Excellencies, not Palace Attendant of the Third Rank.

proposals.before: Emperor Wu of Zhou heard and approved; he advanced him to Palace Attendant of the Third Rank, granted him the noble rank of Duke of Xindu County, and promoted him to governor of Yanzhou.
proposals.after: Emperor Wu of Zhou heard and approved; he advanced him to Equal to the Three Excellencies, granted him the noble rank of Duke of Xindu County, and promoted him to governor of Yanzhou.
proposals.reason: 儀同三司 is mistranslated as Palace Attendant of the Third Rank.

proposals.before: Later he followed Wei Xiaokuan against Yuchi Tong and was appointed Grand General, advanced to Duke of Wushan Commandery.
proposals.after: Later he followed Wei Xiaokuan against Yuchi Jiong and was appointed Grand General, advanced to Duke of Wushan Commandery.
proposals.reason: 尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong, not Tong.

proposals.before: Later he followed Wei Xiaokuan in campaigning against Yuchi Tong; for merit he was appointed Grand General and advanced to Duke of Wushan Commandery.
proposals.after: Later he followed Wei Xiaokuan in campaigning against Yuchi Jiong; for merit he was appointed Grand General and advanced to Duke of Wushan Commandery.
proposals.reason: 尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong, not Tong.

proposals.before: Lying ill with rage, Shi was visited by his son Xin, then a Palace Attendant of the Same Rank, who wept and said, "Father, you are a senior minister of the court and have committed no grave fault. Many nobles have been dismissed and humiliated only to return to office shortly thereafter. How can you remain in such despair?
proposals.after: Lying ill with rage, Shi was visited by his son Xin, then Equal to the Three Excellencies, who wept and said, "Father, you are a senior minister of the court and have committed no grave fault. Many nobles have been dismissed and humiliated only to return to office shortly thereafter. How can you remain in such despair?
proposals.reason: 儀同 is the rank Yitong, not Palace Attendant of the Same Rank.

proposals.before: Shi lay ill with rage; his son Xin, then a Palace Attendant of the Same Rank, came before Shi weeping and said: "Father, you are already a great minister of the court and have committed no great fault—lately one sees many nobles dismissed and humiliated who soon return to external appointment; how can you remain thus for long?
proposals.after: Shi lay ill with rage; his son Xin, then Equal to the Three Excellencies, came before Shi weeping and said: "Father, you are already a great minister of the court and have committed no great fault—lately one sees many nobles dismissed and humiliated who soon return to external appointment; how can you remain thus for long?
proposals.reason: 儀同 is mistranslated as Palace Attendant of the Same Rank.

proposals.before: When Xuan Gan rebelled, Hongsi stationed troops at Anding.
proposals.after: When Xuangan rebelled, Hongsi stationed troops at Anding.
proposals.reason: 玄感 is a single given name; splitting it as Xuan Gan obscures the referent.

proposals.before: Someone reported that he plotted to join Xuan Gan; the Prince of Dai You sent men to seize him and escort him to the imperial residence.
proposals.after: Someone reported that he plotted to join Xuangan; the Prince of Dai, You, sent men to seize him and escort him to the imperial residence.
proposals.reason: 玄感 should remain one name; 代王侑 is Prince of Dai named You, not a person Dai You.

proposals.before: When Wentong took office he heard the man's name and had him arrested.
proposals.after: When Wentong took office he heard the man's name and rebuked him.
proposals.reason: 數之 here means to enumerate charges and rebuke, not to arrest; the arrest and torture follow in the next sentence.

proposals.before: When Wentong took up his post he heard the man's name and had him counted and punished.
proposals.after: When Wentong took up his post he heard the man's name and rebuked him.
proposals.reason: 數之 is rebuke or listing of faults, not numerical counting or a completed punishment.

decisions.reason: 殆與郅、寧之倫異乎 is a rhetorical question of contrast: these officials’ 禁奸除猾 differed from Zhi Du and Ning Cheng, who crushed real villains, whereas the preceding sentences say they flogged the innocent. The original “scarcely differed” inverts that meaning; the proposed rendering is accurate.
殿中尚書 is the Northern Wei Palace Minister, not an Attendant Secretary, and 叔孫侯頭 is the full personal name Shusun Houtou, confirmed by the next sentence’s 侯頭.
The same office and name errors as the idiomatic line: 殿中尚書 and 侯頭.
北平陽尼 names Yang Ni of Beiping commandery; 北平 is not “northern Pingcheng” (平城).
北平 is the commandery Beiping; splitting it as Pingcheng in the north invents 平城.
就家賜盡 is a bestowed death or ordered suicide at home, not specifically strangulation; the idiomatic line already has the broader sense.
賜爵安陽男 is the rank nan (baron), not hou (marquis); the biography later uses 侯 for Marquis of Rencheng.
男 is baron, not marquis.
獻文親舅 means he was styled Emperor Xianwen’s maternal uncle (via Empress Yuan calling him brother), not the empress dowager’s uncle.
河西都將 is a Hexi campaign commander (dujiang), not 大將軍 “General-in-Chief.”
子神 is kinship 子 plus the given name 神, not a binome Zi Shen; the next unit is 長子神.
子 marks “son”; 神 is the personal name.
After 劉氏四子 and 子神, 長子神 is “the eldest son, Shen,” not a native of Changzi county.
The chapter’s 武卉中郎 is a graphic corruption of 武賁/虎賁中郎. Weishu writes 初為虎賁中郎; Rapid-as-Tigers Palace Gentleman is the correct office, not a title Wuhui.
Paired with 靈丘, 應門 is a corruption of 雁門 (Yanmen), the neighboring commandery in the capital region. Weishu has 於靈丘、雁門間聚為劫害.

sourceWitness.excerpt: 於靈丘、雁門間聚為劫害

decisions.reason: 襄城長公主 is the rank 長公主 (Grand Princess of Xiangcheng), not a personal name Chang.
長公主 is a rank, not the given name Chang.
襲祖爵 is inheritance of the grandfather’s noble rank (武津縣公 of Cui Xuan), not the father’s; Zan received only a posthumous governorship.
祖爵 denotes the grandfather’s title, not the father’s.
馮翊下邽 is Xiagui in Fengyi, not Xiayi (下邑).
下邽 is Xiagui, not Xiayi.
儀同三司 is the prestige rank Equal to the Three Excellencies, not Palace Attendant of the Third Rank.
儀同三司 is mistranslated as Palace Attendant of the Third Rank.
尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong; Tong misreads 迥.
尉遲迥 is Yuchi Jiong, not Tong.
時為儀同 abbreviates 儀同三司 (Equal to the Three Excellencies / Yitong), not Palace Attendant of the Same Rank.
儀同 is the same prestige rank, not Palace Attendant of the Same Rank.
玄感 is one given name (Xuangan); splitting it as Xuan Gan obscures the rebel named in the idiomatic line as Yang Xuan'gan.
玄感 remains one name; 代王侑 is the Prince of Dai, personal name You, not a person named Dai You.
聞其名而數之 is to enumerate faults and rebuke; arrest and torture begin in the next sentence (因令剡木為大橛). “Had him arrested” invents an action not in this unit.
數之 is rebuke or listing of charges, not numerical counting or a completed punishment.

claimRevisions.reason: The English personal name Shusun Hou was produced by truncating 侯頭; the repair restores Shusun Houtou.
The English office Wuhui was an artifact of reading 武卉 as a place-name; Weishu shows the post is 虎賁中郎.
Yingmen was created by translating the corrupt 應門; the pairing with Lingqiu is Yanmen.
